transcript:
Meeting header: Date/Time: 2028-02-13 16:00 UTC | Duration: 54 min | Location: Zoom | Recording: Yes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Ramos (Redwood SE), Aisha Patel (Springboard Head of ML), Tom Rivers (Platform), Dr. Elena Kovalchuk (Research)

Summary: High-level discovery focused on model selection for biologics research assistant, strong need for long context (20k-50k), multilingual support for English/Russian, tool-calling for internal knowledge base and secure retrieval, and strict data residency/HIPAA needs. Customer evaluating Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private.

[00:00] Maya Chen: hey everyone thanks for joining, i'm maya from Redwood, i'll kick us off. quick intro and agenda, we want to understand your workloads and constraints and then walk through model choices and deployment options.
[00:22] Aisha Patel: thanks, maya. i'm aisha, we run the ml team at Springboard. quick context: we're building an assistant for research scientists to summarize experiments and pull from internal lab notebooks, some of which are in russian. privacy is huge for us cause a lot of this ties to clinical trial prep.
[00:40] Tom Rivers: yeah and from infra side we need guidance on whether hosted is feasible for POC or we have to go dedicated/private because of data residency and kms integration.
[00:55] Diego Ramos: cool. two quick q's: typical doc lengths / context you expect, and traffic patterns for inference?
[01:08] Aisha Patel: doc bundles can be 30k tokens on average, sometimes up to 70k for concatenated lab notes. traffic is bursty — a few hundred requests an hour during daytime, but with spikes when new study data lands.
[01:26] Maya Chen: got it. so we're looking at multi-10k context models or a retrieval + tool-calling approach with KV cache / prefix caching. what are your SLAs for latency?
[01:40] Elena Kovalchuk: for interactive use, under 1.5s for short answers, but for long summarization we can tolerate 6-8s. Accuracy on technical language is more important than sub-second latencies.
[01:56] Tom Rivers: and security: SOC2 is baseline, HIPAA required for certain datasets, plus we need to manage our own keys ideally.
[02:08] Diego Ramos: understood. on model selection, we usually weigh open models like Mistral/Starcoder-ish families versus instruction-tuned Llama derivatives. for long context and multilinguality, there are two main patterns: native long-context models (32k/65k) or retrieval + chunking with tool-calling to your secure vector DB. each has tradeoffs on cost, latency, and hallucination.
[02:34] Aisha Patel: curious about hallucination — for us false claims on experimental results are a non-starter. does redwood provide eval hooks?
[02:45] Maya Chen: yes — Redwood Optimize includes quality monitoring and regression alerts tied to your prompt sets. we can run evals on your sample prompts and flag divergence between model variants.
[02:58] [00:03:00] Speaker 4: (brief crosstalk)
[03:10] Elena Kovalchuk: the russian text sometimes includes domain-specific abbreviations; we need good tokenization support and ideally a model that handles cyrillic well. any idea which open models are best?
[03:25] Diego Ramos: model candidates: a couple that handle multilingual are Mistral-X variants, and some Llama2/Llama3 derivatives that have been fine-tuned for biomedical text. there are community tuned models too. we should test on your russian subset. also note replicates and anthro— actually anthro-prompting shows good safety layers but often higher cost.
[03:46] Aisha Patel: are there quantized options for Dedicated to save cost? we expect heavy token volumes.
[03:53] Diego Ramos: yes, in Dedicated you can run 4-bit/8-bit quantized variants. Redwood's runtime supports quantization-friendly execution paths and we can advise per workload. that usually reduces memory and cost but may slightly alter output distribution; we'll include quality checks.
[04:12] Tom Rivers: on the private deployment side — can we do an air-gapped on-prem run? we have a lab that requires that for PHI at times.
[04:20] Maya Chen: yes, Redwood Private supports on-prem packages and customer-managed networking. we integrate with customer KMS/HSM and keep audit logs for compliance. we also offer a private control plane option if you want a thin network boundary.
[04:35] Elena Kovalchuk: how about tool-calling — we want the model to call an internal retrieval tool and a calculation microservice for certain units conversion.
[04:44] Diego Ramos: tool-calling is supported — function-calling style or structured output. we can route calls to your internal endpoints via secure connectors in Dedicated or via VPC peering for Private. for Hosted we do secure webhooks but that may not satisfy your registry requirements.
[05:01] Aisha Patel: and latency on tool-calls? if the call to retrieval is slow, we can't block UI.
[05:09] Diego Ramos: we recommend async tool-calling patterns with streaming partial responses, and Redwood Console lets you observe end-to-end traces per request. fallback policies are also configurable — e.g., return best-effort summary when retrieval times out.
[05:26] [00:05:30] Speaker 2: (background noise)
[05:38] Maya Chen: on benchmarking, we propose a 7-day pilot: run the same prompt sets across 3 model variants — native 32k open model, 8k model + retrieval pipeline, and a quantized dedicated variant. benchmark for latency, tokens per request, and hallucination rate against your eval set.
[05:56] Tom Rivers: that would be perfect. what telemetry will you need from our side?
[06:03] Diego Ramos: we'll ask for sample prompt files, a representative doc corpus (can be redacted), and an optional vector DB snapshot or schema. also we'll need access to a small test endpoint or S3 bucket for storing artifacts.
[06:17] Aisha Patel: about pricing — can you give a rough delta between Hosted and Dedicated for 10M tokens/month?
[06:27] Maya Chen: rough ballpark: Hosted with curated open models tends to be higher per-token but no infra commitments; Dedicated gives predictable unit costs and lower per-token when you drive high throughput. I'll share a detailed pricing sheet after the call.
[06:40] Elena Kovalchuk: any past customers in biotech/clinical? references could speed our legal review.
[06:47] Maya Chen: yes, we have a couple of regulated customers — i'll include anonymized case studies and the relevant compliance artifacts.
[06:55] [00:07:00] Aisha Patel: timeline — we want a POC in the next 4 weeks if possible. legal will want SOC2 reports and a draft data processing addendum.
[07:08] Tom Rivers: and for pilot infra, if we do Dedicated, what's min commit?
[07:15] Maya Chen: Dedicated has flexible reserve options — we can do a short-term reserved pool for the pilot. minimal commitment depends on GPU type; i'll include options in the pricing doc.
[07:27] Diego Ramos: technical note: for very long contexts beyond 64k we recommend a hybrid retrieval + chunking pattern; native 100k contexts aren't common in production yet and cost quickly balloons. also be careful with KV cache warmup for large prefix lengths.
[07:48] Aisha Patel: understood. could you also test hallucination on a set of patient-note style prompts?
[07:54] Diego Ramos: yes we'll include that in the benchmark. any preferences for evaluation metrics? F1 on entity extraction, factual consistency, and a domain-specific correctness score?
[08:07] Elena Kovalchuk: yes those three. and include russian-language metrics where appropriate.
[08:16] Maya Chen: great. i'll summarize next steps: diego runs the benchmarks, maya sends pricing/security docs and references, aisha provides data samples and prompts.
[08:26] Aisha Patel: sounds good. thanks team.
[08:29] Tom Rivers: one more Q — do you provide SSO/SAML and RBAC for console access?
[08:34] Maya Chen: yes SSO/SAML, SCIM provisioning, role-based access and token-level auditing.
[08:40] [00:09:00] Speaker 1: (murmur)
[08:45] Maya Chen: any blockers from your legal side we should prep for?
[08:48] Tom Rivers: legal will want a draft DPA and to understand data flows for the Hosted option. if we go Private they'd want the Air-gap playbook.
[08:58] Maya Chen: noted. we'll include diagrams in the playbook.
[09:02] Elena Kovalchuk: ok wrapping up — do you have anything else to surface?
[09:05] Diego Ramos: just one more technical caveat: for Russian cyrillic tokenization we may need to test different tokenizer models; sometimes chunk boundaries break words leading to omission. we'll include tokenizer sensitivity in the eval.
[09:22] Aisha Patel: excellent. thanks everyone.

Recap: 1) Redwood to run 7-day benchmark comparing native long-context vs retrieval+8k model vs quantized dedicated run. 2) Redwood to provide pricing and compliance docs. 3) Springboard to provide sample prompts and doc corpus.

Shared artifacts mentioned: Redwood pilot plan deck (link: https://redwood.example.com/decks/sb-pilot), benchmark sheet (link: https://redwood.example.com/benchmarks/sb-32k-vs-retrieval.xlsx), SOC2/HIPAA pack (link: https://redwood.example.com/compliance/sb-pack).

End of transcript.
